title: Data outlives code: rolling upgrades and migrations
goal: By the end, you can explain why updating a program means running two versions at once over the same data, show how an old version erases a field it doesn't know and fix it, say what went wrong at Knight Capital, and change what a database column means in steps that never break a running version.
opening:
Picture the owner of a bookshop in Berlin. Every evening she checks her card payments in an app from the company that handles them. One morning the app offers a new setting, and she switches its language to German. By lunchtime it's back in English. She sets German again. Two days later, English again. Nobody touched her settings, and nothing logged an error.

It's easy to think of an update as a moment: the old version stops and the new one starts. From outside, that's how it looks. Inside, for minutes or days, both versions run side by side over the same stored data, and both write.

In Schemas that evolve, old code met a field it had never seen and skipped it. In this lesson, we'll run two versions of one program over one table and watch the old one erase what the new one wrote. Then we'll look at a firm that lost $460 million to a mix of versions, and change a column without breaking either. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.

warmup.q: The payments company runs its program on ten machines, and it's in the middle of an update: 9 machines run version 2, which adds a language setting to each shop's saved settings, and 1 still runs version 1. Version 1 reads the settings into a class with no language field, changes the shop's status, and saves the class back. After a shop sets its language, its settings get 5 more updates, each on a random machine. Roughly what share of the languages set during the update survive?
options: About 90%, the share of machines on version 2
About 59%
100%, because version 1 ignores fields it doesn't know
0%, because version 1 rejects settings it can't read
warmup.why: The language survives only if all 5 updates land on version 2: 0.9 x 0.9 x 0.9 x 0.9 x 0.9 is about 0.59. Every update on version 1 reads the settings into a class with no language field and saves that class back, so a single touch by version 1 erases it. "Ignore fields it doesn't know" means "don't fail", not "keep them", which makes the third option tempting and wrong. The second section shows the mechanism and the fix.

sections.h: Data outlives code, and an update runs two versions at once
sections.body:
Let's look at what an update replaces, and what it leaves alone. The payments company keeps its data in PostgreSQL, a database program that stores data in tables: rows and columns, like a spreadsheet. One table, `payouts`, has a row for every payment the company has made to a shop. Some rows were written last night, and some in 2019.

An update replaces the program in a few minutes, and each new version that ships is called a release. The update doesn't touch those rows. Each row keeps the shape it was written in, and its encoding (the way it was turned into bytes), until something rewrites it. **Data outlives code.** Writing a row is sending a message to a future version of your own program.

So new code must read rows written by old code. That's backward compatibility, from Schemas that evolve: new code reading old data. In a database it isn't optional, because there is always old data.

The other direction, forward compatibility, means old code reading new data. It's needed too, because of how programs are updated. Say the payout program runs as six copies on six machines, called instances, with a load balancer in front that hands each request to one of them. A **rolling upgrade** replaces them one at a time. It starts an instance of version 2, waits until a health check (a small test request) says it's ready, stops an instance of version 1, and repeats. For those minutes, some requests are served by v1 and some by v2, against the same tables. A row that v2 writes can be read by v1 a second later.

Other habits stretch that overlap. A canary release runs the new version on a few instances for a day before the rest. A batch job, a program that runs once a night over a big pile of rows, may still be on last month's version. And a rollback, putting the old version back after a bad update, is an update in the other direction. Planned or not, you get a mixed-version fleet: instances of different versions, running at the same moment over the same data.

Databases help by putting work off. In PostgreSQL, `ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN` adds a column. When the new column has no default value, or a constant one, it only changes the table's description in the system catalog, the database's own list of tables and columns. Old rows aren't touched; PostgreSQL fills in the default when it reads them. Since PostgreSQL 11, that holds even for `NOT NULL DEFAULT 'EUR'`, a column that must always have a value and gets 'EUR' when none is given.

A volatile default, one that changes from call to call, is different. The current time from `clock_timestamp()` is one. Every row needs its own value, so PostgreSQL rewrites the whole table, and its indexes (the lookup structures that find rows fast), into a new file. All the while it holds an exclusive lock, which keeps every other program from reading or writing the table. The Try it shows both on a million rows.

What the database can't do for you is change what data means. Turning euros into cents, splitting one field into two, or moving data into a table of its own all mean rewriting rows, while code that expects the old shape is still running. The rest of this lesson is about doing that without breaking either version. Keep this picture: a timeline of program versions that overlap two at a time, over data that spans all of them.

Next, we'll watch the most common way that overlap loses data.

try.title: Add a column to a million rows, twice
steps: From the `labs` folder, start PostgreSQL 18 with `docker compose -f env/postgres.yml up -d --wait`. (Docker runs programs in containers, small sealed-off spaces; this command starts the database in one.) Then open psql, PostgreSQL's command-line window, with `docker compose -f env/postgres.yml exec db psql -U sfz`.
Create a million-row `payouts` table and note its file number, the name of the file that holds it on disk. Then add a column with a constant default (block below).
Predict before the last ALTER: will a `clock_timestamp()` default change the file number? How long will it take, compared with the first ALTER?
Keep the prompt and the table open: the Try its in the third and fourth sections use them.

code.title: psql, database sfz

try.expect:
```text
 file  | size
-------+-------
 16385 | 56 MB

ALTER TABLE
Time: 1.336 ms
 file
-------
 16385

 id | amount | currency
----+--------+----------
  1 |   0.07 | EUR

ALTER TABLE
Time: 731.523 ms
 file  | size
-------+-------
 16393 | 65 MB
```
(blank lines and row counts trimmed; your file numbers and times will differ). The constant default took about a millisecond and left the same file. The million old rows weren't touched, and PostgreSQL fills in `EUR` when it reads them. The `clock_timestamp()` default rewrote every row into a new, bigger file, and held an exclusive lock the whole time. On a 50 GB table, that's minutes in which nothing else can use it.

sections.h: Old code that saves a record back deletes what it doesn't know
sections.body:
Here is the most common way a mixed fleet loses data. The company's customers are the shops, and each one has a settings document, stored as JSON in a `jsonb` column (PostgreSQL's column type for JSON). Version 2 adds `preferredLanguage`, and a settings screen to set it. Version 1 has never heard of it, and handles a status update like this:

```kotlin
data class CustomerV1(val id: Int, val name: String, val status: String)

fun updateStatus(stored: String, status: String): String {
    val c: CustomerV1 = mapper.readValue(stored)        // preferredLanguage has nowhere to go
    return mapper.writeValueAsString(c.copy(status = status))
}
```

`CustomerV1` is version 1's class for a shop's settings. `mapper` is an `ObjectMapper` from Jackson, a library many Java and Kotlin programs use to read and write JSON. `readValue` turns the JSON into a `CustomerV1`, `copy` makes a copy with a new status, and `writeValueAsString` turns it back into JSON.

Plain Jackson fails on a field the class doesn't have, which would at least be loud. But Quarkus and Spring Boot, two popular toolkits for building Java programs, both set up their `ObjectMapper` to ignore unknown fields. So the decode succeeds, the language is dropped, and the encode writes a document without it. Nothing logs anything. That's the bookshop's German setting, and the stepper below walks through it.

How much is lost? Say a shop sets a language on v2, the only version with that screen. Then it gets five status updates, each on a random instance. The language survives only if all five land on v2. With 90% of the fleet on v2, that's 0.9 to the power of 5, about 59%, so 41% of the languages set during the rollout are gone. At 50%, about 97% are gone. The Try it simulates exactly this, and so does the lab.

**A program that saves a whole record erases what it doesn't know. Change only what you own.** Read the document as a tree, Jackson's `ObjectNode`, a map of whatever fields the JSON has. Set `status` and write the tree back, so fields you don't know ride along. Or don't read and write the whole document at all. SQL is the language programs use to talk to a database, and this SQL command changes one key inside the database: `UPDATE customers SET doc = jsonb_set(doc, '{status}', '"active"') WHERE id = ?`.

Protobuf does the first for you, since protobuf-java keeps unknown fields and writes them back (Schemas that evolve). Avro doesn't. Decode with v1's reader's schema, encode with it again, and the new field is gone.

The same trap appears without JSON columns. A cache that stores whole v1 objects drops new fields the same way. So does a Kafka consumer, a program that reads messages from a log, if it reads a message, adds something and sends it on. A library that maps each row to an object (an ORM) is mostly safe for a new column it doesn't know, because its `UPDATE` never mentions that column. But a v1 `INSERT`, the command that adds a row, leaves the new column empty, NULL in SQL's words, which the last section's migration has to handle.

Next, we'll see what a mixed fleet did to one firm in 45 minutes.

sections.h: Knight Capital: one server on old code, one flag with a new meaning
sections.body:
On 1 August 2012, Knight Capital lost more than $460 million in about 45 minutes. Knight was a large US firm that bought and sold shares, small pieces of a company that people trade, all day, for its customers and for itself. The SEC, the US agency that oversees share trading, set out what happened in a 2013 order, and the cause is a mixed-version fleet.

Knight's program for sending orders to buy and sell shares to the stock exchanges, called SMARS, ran on eight servers (computers that run programs for others). For a new program at the New York Stock Exchange, the Retail Liquidity Program (RLP), developers wrote new code. They also reused a **flag**, a yes-or-no marker in each order that switches some code on. It had once switched on an old feature called Power Peg. Knight had stopped using Power Peg in 2003, but its code was still in SMARS and could still run. In 2005, someone moved the part of the code that counted how many shares of an order had been traded, and nobody tested Power Peg again. Starting on 27 July, Knight installed the RLP code in stages over several days. A technician didn't copy it to one of the eight servers, and no second person checked the work.

On 1 August, orders arrived with the flag set. Seven servers ran the new RLP code correctly. The eighth ran Power Peg. With its counter gone, Power Peg kept sending smaller orders, and never noticed that the original order was complete. For 212 customer orders it sent millions: 4 million trades in 154 stocks, more than 397 million shares. Knight was left holding about $3.5 billion of shares it had bought, and owing about $3.15 billion of shares it had sold without owning them.

While trying to fix it, the team removed the new code from the seven good servers. The flag still arrived, Power Peg was still there, and now all eight servers ran it. Earlier that morning, 97 automatic emails had reported "Power Peg disabled" before the market opened. They weren't designed as alerts, and staff generally didn't read them. The SEC fined Knight $12 million.

Take away the trading, and three points carry over to any program:

- A staged update is a mixed-version fleet. One server out of eight was a 12.5% rollout that nobody knew about, and the rollback was another update that made it 100%.
- Reusing a flag is reusing a Protobuf field number, from Schemas that evolve. The bits stay the same, the meaning changes, and old code acts on the old meaning without an error. Flags, status codes, enum values (named choices from a fixed list) and columns all count.
- Old code that can still run is part of what you must stay compatible with. Delete it, and let a full release go by before anything reuses what it used.

**An old name with a new meaning is a trap for every old reader. Give a new meaning a new name.**

The database version of the flag is changing what a column means in place. `ALTER TABLE refunds ALTER COLUMN amount TYPE bigint USING (amount * 100)::bigint` turns euros into cents in one statement (`bigint` is PostgreSQL's 64-bit whole number). Every v1 instance still running keeps inserting `40.00`, meaning forty euros. PostgreSQL stores it in the new column as 40, which now means forty cents. Nobody gets an error.

Next, we'll make the same change in steps that never break either version.

try.title: Change a column's meaning in place, then watch v1 write
steps: In the psql prompt from the first section, run the block below. The `ALTER` is v2's migration, the script that changes the table for v2. The second `INSERT` comes from a v1 instance that hasn't been replaced yet.
Predict the two amounts before you look.

code.title: psql, database sfz

try.expect:
```text
 id | amount
----+--------
  1 |   4000
  2 |     40
```
Both refunds were 40 euros. Row 2 now reads as 40 cents, and every statement succeeded: PostgreSQL rounds a decimal into a `bigint` column without complaint. The fix is never to change a column's meaning in place. Add `amount_minor` next to it, as in the last section.

sections.h: Change the schema in phases: expand, migrate, contract
sections.body:
Back to `payouts`. Its `amount` column holds euros as `numeric(12,2)`, an exact decimal with two digits after the point. You want `amount_minor`, a `bigint` of cents, like every other money field in the company. The quick way is one migration, a script that changes the database's tables, which renames and converts the column and ships with the update. The lab tries it. The moment it runs, every v1 instance still in the fleet fails with `column "amount" does not exist` (SQLSTATE 42703, PostgreSQL's code for that error) until the rollout ends. Stopping the program first avoids the errors, but the downtime, the time the program is switched off, grows with the table. Stripe, a large payments company, worked out that moving 100 million records at one per second would take more than three years.

What works is **expand and contract**, also called parallel change. First, expand the schema so it holds the old shape and the new one at the same time. Then move readers and writers across, one rollout at a time. Then contract the schema to the new shape. Stripe described its version in a 2017 post about moving hundreds of millions of subscriptions (regular payments, such as a monthly plan) into a table of their own. It has four phases: dual-write (write both the old and the new place), switch reads, switch writes, and remove the old data. For `payouts`, it takes six steps:

1. Expand: `ALTER TABLE payouts ADD COLUMN amount_minor bigint`. It may be empty and has no default, so it only changes the catalog. v1's inserts, which don't mention it, keep working.
2. Deploy v2, which writes both columns in one statement and still reads `amount`. While v1 and v2 overlap, a v1 instance can change `amount` on a row v2 has just written, which leaves `amount_minor` out of date.
3. Backfill, after the last v1 instance is gone: copy `round(amount * 100)` into `amount_minor` wherever it's NULL or different. Do it in batches of a few thousand rows, each in its own short transaction, a group of changes that succeed or fail together. Then locks and the WAL stay small. The WAL is the log where PostgreSQL first writes every change.
4. Deploy v3, which reads `amount_minor`. Stripe ran the old and the new read side by side and logged every difference, with Scientist, a library from GitHub, the code-sharing site. That's called a shadow read. The lab's v3 counts mismatches the same way.
5. Let `amount` be NULL and make `amount_minor` NOT NULL (never empty), then deploy v4, which writes only `amount_minor`. PostgreSQL 18 can add that rule as `NOT VALID`, which checks only new rows, and check the existing rows later with `VALIDATE CONSTRAINT`. That takes a weaker lock, so reads and writes go on.
6. Contract: once no running version mentions `amount`, drop it.

**Every step must work with the versions on both sides of it.** That's the whole trick, and the figure shows it. Each schema step is its own Flyway migration. (Flyway is a tool that runs numbered migration scripts in order; the SQL track's lesson SQL from the JVM uses it.) So a change that used to be one file becomes a process that takes several updates, and maybe weeks. Ship each contract step one release after the code stopped using the old column, so that rolling back to the version before still works.

One hazard remains: locks. Every `ALTER TABLE` above except `VALIDATE` takes an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock, the strongest kind, even the instant ones. If any open transaction holds a lock on the table, the ALTER waits for it. Every query (a request to read or change data) that arrives after the ALTER then queues behind it. A one-millisecond ALTER behind a forgotten `BEGIN`, a transaction someone started and never finished, stops all reads of the table. Set `lock_timeout` to a few seconds before you change a busy table, and retry when it fails.

Here is where the method stops. It needs several releases, a backfill that may run for hours, and a team that knows what each version may touch. Nothing in the database enforces the order.

try.title: Watch an instant ALTER block every read
steps: Open three psql prompts on the same database (`docker compose -f env/postgres.yml exec db psql -U sfz`, in three terminal windows), called A, B and C below.
In A, start a transaction that reads `payouts`, and leave it open: `BEGIN; SELECT count(*) FROM payouts;`
In B, run `ALTER TABLE payouts ADD COLUMN amount_minor bigint;`. In C, run `SELECT amount FROM payouts WHERE id = 42;`. Both hang.
In a fourth prompt, or in A, look at who waits (query below). Then type `COMMIT;` in A, and watch B and C finish.

Repeat with a timeout: start A's transaction again, and in B run `SET lock_timeout = '2s';` before `ALTER TABLE payouts ADD COLUMN fee_minor bigint;`. Then `COMMIT;` in A. When you're done, `DROP TABLE payouts, refunds;` and stop the database with `docker compose -f env/postgres.yml down`.

code.title: who is waiting for whom
code.src:
SELECT pid, state, wait_event_type AS wait, left(query, 50) AS query
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE datname = 'sfz' AND pid <> pg_backend_pid()
ORDER BY backend_start;

try.expect:
```text
 pid |        state        |  wait  |                       query
-----+---------------------+--------+----------------------------------------------------
 191 | idle in transaction | Client | SELECT count(*) FROM payouts;
 200 | active              | Lock   | ALTER TABLE payouts ADD COLUMN amount_minor2 bigin
 207 | active              | Lock   | SELECT amount FROM payouts WHERE id = 42
```
(captured with a slightly different column name; your pids, the numbers of the database's processes, will differ). A holds a lock that lets others read. B wants an exclusive one and waits. C's plain read waits behind B, because PostgreSQL queues lock requests in order. With the timeout, B gives up instead, and C never waits:
```text
ERROR:  canceling statement due to lock timeout
Time: 2001.270 ms (00:02.001)
```

compare.title: Renaming a column in one step, and in phases

a.label: In one step
a.title: V3__amount_in_cents.sql
a.src:
-- runs when the first v2 instance starts
ALTER TABLE payouts RENAME COLUMN amount TO amount_minor;
ALTER TABLE payouts ALTER COLUMN amount_minor TYPE bigint
    USING (amount_minor * 100)::bigint;   -- rewrites the table

-- every v1 instance still running:
-- ERROR: column "amount" does not exist (42703)

b.label: In phases
b.title: one migration per release

compare.note: The one-step version is shorter, but it takes an exclusive lock for a full rewrite of the table, breaks every old instance at once, and can't be rolled back. The phased version never has a moment when a running version and the schema disagree. Every step is quick, except the backfill, which runs in small transactions while traffic goes on.

worked.title: Write the payouts migration as Flyway files and a backfill job

steps.say: Release 2 ships the expand migration with the code that writes both columns. `SET LOCAL` limits the timeout to the migration's own transaction, so a long transaction on `payouts` makes the update fail and retry, instead of freezing the table.

The backfill is a job, not a migration: it may run for hours, and it must be safe to stop and restart. It starts only after the last v1 instance is gone. Each batch is its own transaction, and the `WHERE` clause finds the work that's left, so a restart carries on where it stopped.

Release 4 switches writes. Split the constraint, the NOT NULL rule, into two migrations. Flyway runs each file in one transaction, and the ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock from `ADD CONSTRAINT` would otherwise be held for the whole check of every row.
Release 5, at least one release after v4 is everywhere, contracts. By then no running version, and no version you might roll back to, mentions `amount`.

lab.title: Measure field loss in a rolling upgrade, then migrate a live table with expand and contract
steps: Run the tests once from the `labs` folder. All 12 fail. The first run downloads `postgres:18`, the package Docker uses to start PostgreSQL 18, if you don't have it; after that the database starts in a few seconds.
In `FieldLoss.kt`, write `PreservingCodec`: read the JSON as an `ObjectNode`, put the new status, and write it back.

Write `RollingUpgrade.lossRate`. Create the documents, set every language through `V2`, then send each shop's updates to v2 or v1 with `Random(seed)`, and count the documents without a language. The six `FieldLossTest` tests should pass now, including the `1 - p^5` curve.

In `Payouts.kt`, write `Migration.expand`, `PayoutsV2.save` (one statement that inserts or updates a row and writes both columns), `Migration.backfillBatch` and `Migration.contract`. `PayoutsV1`, `PayoutsV3`, `PayoutsV4` and `prepareSwitchWrites` are complete; read them first.

Run the tests until all 12 pass. `ExpandContractTest` runs each rollout as 400 interleaved requests on two versions. It checks for zero errors and zero wrong reads, and checks that a backfill or contract done too early does break things.
hints: `mapper.readTree(stored) as ObjectNode` gives you a tree you can change; `put("status", newStatus)` returns the same node.
Route each update with `if (rnd.nextInt(100) < v2Percent) V2.touch(doc, "active") else v1.touch(doc, "active")`. Make all the `Random` calls in the same order every run, or the seed won't repeat.

The backfill must also fix rows where `amount_minor` is set but wrong, because a v1 instance can change `amount` after v2 wrote both. `amount_minor IS DISTINCT FROM round(amount * 100)::bigint` is true for NULL and for wrong values.
If only `ExpandContractTest` fails with a Docker error, start Docker Desktop. `FieldLossTest` needs no Docker.

drill.title: Plan a column rename from memory
drill.prompt: Close the lesson. The `customers` table must rename `email` to `email_address`, with six instances running and no downtime. Write the steps in order: for each one, the SQL (if any), and which program versions run during it. Then check: when does the backfill run, and when is `email` dropped?

answer.src:
1. Expand:   ALTER TABLE customers ADD COLUMN email_address text;     -- v1 runs, unaffected
2. Deploy v2: writes email AND email_address, reads email           -- v1 + v2 overlap
3. Backfill:  UPDATE ... SET email_address = email
              WHERE email_address IS DISTINCT FROM email (batches)  -- only v2 runs
4. Deploy v3: reads email_address, still writes both               -- v2 + v3 overlap
5. ALTER email DROP NOT NULL; email_address NOT NULL (NOT VALID, then VALIDATE)
   Deploy v4: writes only email_address                             -- v3 + v4 overlap
6. One release later: ALTER TABLE customers DROP COLUMN email;      -- only v4 runs
Every ALTER: SET lock_timeout first.

recap: Data outlives code: rows keep the shape they were written in, so new code must read old data (backward compatibility).
A rolling upgrade, a canary release or a rollback runs two versions at once, so old code also reads data written by new code (forward compatibility).

Old code that reads a record into its own class and saves the class back deletes fields it doesn't know. With 5 later updates, a field survives a rollout at p% only with probability p^5. Change only what you own.
Knight Capital lost over $460 million when one of eight servers kept old code and a reused flag switched it on. Never give an old name a new meaning.

Expand and contract changes a schema in steps that each work with the versions on both sides: add, dual-write, backfill, switch reads, switch writes, drop. Set `lock_timeout` before changing a busy table.
The limit: it takes several releases and a careful team, and nothing in the database makes the steps happen in order.
closing:
We started with a bookshop owner whose German setting kept turning back into English. Nothing was broken: version 1 still ran on some machines, and saved her settings back without the language. Every fix in this lesson came down to one rule: each step must work with the versions on both sides of it.

Open your phone's app store, find an app you use every day and look at its version history. Every entry on that list ran side by side with the one before it, on phones and on the company's own machines.

Next, we'll leave the database, have two programs talk over a network, and ask what to do when a call to another program gets no answer.

quiz.q: Version 1 of a program reads stored Protobuf records with protobuf-java 4.x and its normal reader, changes one field and writes each record back. Version 2 has added field 9. What happens to field 9's value?
options: It's dropped, because version 1's generated class has no field 9
It's kept: the reader stores it as an unknown field and writes it back out
The read fails, because field 9 isn't in version 1's schema
It's kept only if version 1 was built with the newest Protobuf compiler
quiz.why: protobuf-java has kept unknown fields by default since 3.5.0, and writes them back out when it encodes, so a read, change and write by old code doesn't lose them. Only a `DiscardUnknownFieldsParser`, or proto3 before 3.5, drops them. The first option is what happens with JSON read into a data class, which has no such safety net: that's this lesson's problem.

quiz.q: 80% of the instances run v2. After a shop sets the new field, its settings get 3 more updates, each on a random instance, and v1 drops unknown fields when it saves. About how many of these values survive?
options: About 80%
About 20%
About 51%
All of them, once the rollout finishes
quiz.why: The value survives only if all 3 updates reach v2: 0.8 x 0.8 x 0.8 is about 0.51. Finishing the rollout stops new losses, but it doesn't bring back values already erased. 80% is the tempting answer if you count only one update.

quiz.q: In an expand and contract migration from `amount` to `amount_minor`, why must the backfill run after the last v1 instance is gone, and fix rows where `amount_minor` differs, not only where it's NULL?
options: Because v1 can still change `amount` on rows that v2 already wrote both ways, leaving `amount_minor` set but out of date
Because PostgreSQL locks the whole table during the backfill
Because v1 would fail on the new column while the backfill runs
Because NULL values can't be updated in batches
quiz.why: Writing both columns protects only the rows that v2 writes. While v1 instances run, they can update `amount` on any row and never touch `amount_minor`, so some rows end up set but wrong. A backfill that runs after v1 is gone, and compares values, fixes them all. Batched UPDATEs lock rows, not the table, and v1 never mentions the new column.

quiz.q: A migration runs `ALTER TABLE payouts ADD COLUMN note text`, which takes a millisecond on its own. On the live database, all reads of `payouts` stop for two minutes. What's the most likely cause?
options: ADD COLUMN rewrites the whole table
The new column made every row larger, so reads got slower
PostgreSQL rebuilds every index on the table after ADD COLUMN
The ALTER waited behind a long open transaction, and every new query queued behind the ALTER's request for an exclusive lock
quiz.why: ADD COLUMN with no default only changes the catalog, but it still needs an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock. While it waits for an old transaction to finish, later reads queue behind it. `SET lock_timeout` makes the ALTER give up and retry instead. A rewrite, the tempting first option, happens only with a volatile default or a type change.

quiz.q: Which change to Knight Capital's process would have stopped that particular failure, even with the missed server?
options: Faster servers, so the runaway orders could be cancelled sooner
Giving RLP a new flag, and deleting Power Peg's code a release before anything reused its flag
Installing the code on all eight servers at the same moment
Sending the 97 automatic emails to a different team
quiz.why: The damage came from old code giving a reused flag its old meaning. With a new flag, the eighth server would have ignored RLP orders' new flag, and with Power Peg deleted there was nothing to trigger. Installing on every server at once still misses servers and still gets rolled back; nobody can update eight machines in the same instant.

flashcards.front: What does "data outlives code" mean for a change to a schema?
flashcards.back: Rows keep the encoding they were written with until something rewrites them, so every version of the code must read every shape still stored.

flashcards.front: Why does a rolling upgrade need forward compatibility?
flashcards.back: While v1 and v2 run side by side over the same database, v1 reads rows that v2 has just written.

flashcards.front: How does old code lose a field it doesn't know?
flashcards.back: It reads the record into its own class (ignoring unknown fields), changes something and saves the whole class back, without the field.

flashcards.front: What are Stripe's four phases for moving data while the system runs?
flashcards.back: Write to both the old and the new place, switch reads to the new, switch writes to the new, then remove the old data.

flashcards.front: Why must the backfill run after the last old-code instance is gone?
flashcards.back: Old code keeps writing only the old column, so rows it touches during or after a backfill go out of date again.

flashcards.front: Why set `lock_timeout` before `ALTER TABLE` on a busy table?
flashcards.back: The ALTER needs an exclusive lock. While it waits behind an open transaction, every later query queues behind it. A timeout makes it fail fast and retry.

flashcards.front: What did the reused flag do at Knight Capital?
flashcards.back: New code used an old flag to mean "use RLP". On the one server still running old code, the flag switched on dead Power Peg code, which sent millions of orders in 45 minutes.

terms.plain: Replacing a program's instances one at a time, so the old and new versions run side by side for a while.
The set of instances running different versions of the code at the same moment, against the same data.
A script, or a planned series of steps, that changes a database's tables and moves the old data to the new shape.
Changing a schema in steps: add the new shape next to the old, move the code over, then remove the old shape. Also called parallel change.
Code that writes both the old and the new column (or table), so that either can be read.
A job that fills the new column for existing rows, in small batches, while the system keeps running.
Reading from both the old and the new place, serving one and logging every difference, to prove the new path is right.
A PostgreSQL setting that makes a statement give up if it can't get its lock in time, instead of waiting and blocking everyone behind it.

explain_back.prompt: A teammate wants to change `payouts.amount` from euros to cents with one `ALTER COLUMN ... TYPE bigint USING amount * 100` in the next release's migration. Explain what goes wrong during the rolling upgrade, and what you'd do instead.
explain_back.answer: The migration runs when the first new instance starts, but the old instances keep running for a while, and they keep writing euros into the same column. 40.00 becomes 40, which the new code reads as 40 cents. Nothing fails, so nobody notices until someone checks the money against the bank. The ALTER also rewrites the whole table under an exclusive lock, and a rollback can't undo the change in meaning. Instead I'd expand and contract. Add a nullable `amount_minor`, which is instant. Ship code that writes both columns. Backfill `amount_minor` in batches once no old instance is left. Ship code that reads `amount_minor`, with a shadow read that compares it with `amount`. Then ship code that writes only `amount_minor`, and drop `amount` a release later. Every step works with the versions on either side, and each ALTER gets a `lock_timeout`.

deeper.body:
Designing Data-Intensive Applications (2nd edition, chapter 5) describes a database as a message to your future self, and calls keeping compatibility across complex migrations an open research problem. Project Cambria (Ink & Switch, 2020) is one research answer: "lenses" that translate each record between schema versions as it's read and written, so old and new code each see their own shape.

**Tools for expand and contract.** Tools now automate parts of the method on PostgreSQL. pgroll, for example, puts a set of views (saved queries that look like tables) over the real tables for each version. It backfills a new column from the old one, and keeps the two in step with triggers, small functions the database runs on every change, until the migration completes. Old and new code each pick their version through `search_path`. For MySQL, another database program, gh-ost and pt-online-schema-change copy the table in the background and switch over at the end. They solve the locking and the copying. They don't solve meaning: deciding that `amount` is euros and `amount_minor` is cents, and that no flag is ever reused, is still your job.

**Ship the contract step late.** A common mistake is to move reads and writes to `amount_minor` in v4, and put `ALTER TABLE payouts DROP COLUMN amount` in the same release's migration. Flyway runs it when the first v4 instance starts, while the others are still v3 and still write `amount`. Every v3 write fails with SQLSTATE 42703 until the rollout ends, and a rollback to v3 is now impossible, because the column is gone. A release must work with the schema of the release before it.

**Stripe's post** is worth reading in full for the parts this lesson skipped: how Stripe used Hadoop jobs over copies of the database to find the records to move, and how it compared millions of reads with Scientist before trusting the new path.
